source.title: Changing the Kernel During Training Leads to Double Descent in Kernel Regression

record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent with kernel regression as model complexity varies by minimum bandwidth, and also reports a neural-network size sweep; these are conceptual tests rather than reproductions of the original experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-error curves against minimum bandwidth and test R² for four neural-network sizes. It does not sweep training sample size or report test error over epochs. The neural-network preconditioning result is not a size- or epoch-wise double-descent curve.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps model complexity (minimum allowed bandwidth σm) in kernel regression on synthetic and four real datasets. It reports test error curves with a peak near zero training error and a second descent for the decreasing-bandwidth scheme (KGD-D), but none for constant-bandwidth KRR. This bears directly on V4. It also gives a four-point feed-forward network size comparison (Figure 3) bearing on V1. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that decreasing a translation-invariant kernel's bandwidth during training yields double descent in minimum allowed bandwidth. Driving the bandwidth to zero gives benign overfitting and beats constant-bandwidth KRR tuned by cross-validation or marginal likelihood maximization. The Laplace kernel is the stated exception. The NTK-modification result for neural networks is explicitly preliminary, and the four-network Figure 3 is illustrative rather than a main result.
record.recipe_differences: Uses kernel regression with a training-time bandwidth schedule and minimum-bandwidth complexity, rather than the original deep-network size and sample-size sweeps. Also includes a four-configuration neural-network size comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The result depends on kernel choice: the Laplace kernel is reported as an exception. For the principal Gaussian-kernel sweep, the study fixes training time/regularization; the bandwidth-decrease schedule is also a method choice.

fits_no_version.finding: A preconditioned network (p=151) whose NTK is made to mimic a bandwidth decreasing to zero interpolates the training data (R²tr=1.00) with test R²=0.95. It converges in 1.5e4 epochs, versus up to 1e7 for standard training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changing the NTK during training so it mimics a shrinking bandwidth yields benign overfitting in neural networks.

record.problems: The neural-network size evidence is a sparse four-configuration comparison, and no uncertainty is stated for those test R² values. Many bandwidth-curve values are figure-only. The reported double-descent result is specifically for changing bandwidth during training and does not generalize to the Laplace kernel in the reported experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the real-data constant-bandwidth comparator curves for Matérn ν=3/2, Matérn ν=5/2, and Cauchy in Figure 7; Appendix E states these non-Laplace-kernel results agree with Figure 4. Also omitted training-error curves and the neural-network preconditioned-gradient example because they do not measure test-error double descent across the claim versions.

untested.parts: There is no dense or controlled width sweep; peak location relative to the interpolation threshold is not established. Only one small synthetic dataset with n=20 is used.
No test error over training epochs is reported.
Only kernel regression with a bandwidth axis is tested, at a fixed λ=0.001. Other model classes and ridgeless interpolation are not tested.
The bound explains the peak via ∆k2 and smin, but no single complexity measure is tested for predicting the peak location across axes.
Label noise and regularization strength are not varied; there is no test of multiple peaks or of the peak vanishing under optimal regularization.
Effective degrees of freedom are discussed theoretically (Appendix A). No curve is re-plotted against effective parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The double descent shown is specific to a training-time bandwidth schedule. With a fixed bandwidth, KRR shows only the classical overfitting rise, so the second descent depends on the training procedure. The V1 evidence is one illustrative figure with no uncertainty, and the architectures also differ in depth and epochs trained. All V4 bandwidth-sweep rows are figure-only, with verbal descriptions in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Only four feed-forward neural-network configurations are compared; the study does not provide a dense size sweep or establish a general peak location.
No test-error curve over training epochs or training time.
No sweep that increases the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
Tests kernel regression as minimum bandwidth varies, not a broad range of model classes.
Does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Noise and regularization are not systematically varied to test peak causes, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimal regularization.
Discusses effective degrees of freedom and bandwidth, but does not test whether re-counting complexity turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.reason: Test R² goes 0.21→0.85→0.41→0.68, a fall-rise-fall in test error, with the peak at the first interpolating model (r1–r4). The evidence is sparse and depth and epochs are confounded.
relationships.display_finding: Test R² changed from 0.21 to 0.85 to 0.41 to 0.68, implying an error peak at the first interpolating model, although depth and training duration also varied.
